source.title: RIGA at SemEval-2023 Task 2: NER Enhanced with GPT-3

record.tranche_reason: Applies scaling in a new setting—fine-tuned NER—and reports downstream F1 outcomes for different model sizes and training durations. It does not reproduce the original held-out-loss measurements or fit scaling laws.
record.gate_note: The paper reports validation NER F1 comparisons, not held-out pretraining cross-entropy, fitted power laws, extrapolation tests, or compute-optimal parameter/token allocations. Rows are limited to reported results comparing model size or training duration; other NER-method and context results do not test the scaling claim.
record.test_reason: This is a SemEval NER system paper. It invokes Kaplan-style 'scaling laws' as a design heuristic: swap BERT-base for XLM-R-large and train longer. It reports only its own system's validation F1. There is no loss measurement, no curve over scale and no predictability test. The size comparisons are two-point and confounded: different pretrained models (English uncased BERT vs multilingual XLM-R, with different pretraining data and compute), plus hyperparameter tuning in the best run. The 'compute' scaling is fine-tuning duration (removing early stopping), not pretraining scale. None of its results can show whether downstream performance improves predictably with scale or pretraining loss.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors conclude that GPT-3-mined context markedly improves NER: about 4 points on validation and about 17 points on the official test. They also conclude that 'utilizing the scaling laws' (scaling at least two of data, parameters, compute) boosts system performance. They add that scaling compute alone did not help with adapters. They say it works when trainable parameters, not total parameters, are scaled. These are informal assertions from their own system runs, not tested scaling-law results.
record.recipe_differences: This is a downstream NER fine-tuning study using validation F1, with model-size and training-duration comparisons; it does not use the original held-out language-model loss measurements or fit the original scaling laws.
record.method_sensitivity: Reported outcomes vary with model size, adapter versus full fine-tuning, early stopping versus longer training, and hyperparameter tuning. The study also reports effects of added context, but those results are not scaling-law measurements.

fits_no_version.finding: For full fine-tuning of BERT-base, disabling early stopping raised validation NER F1 from 61.2% to 69.9%. For adapter training, the same change left F1 unchanged (63.4% both). The authors say F1 did not track validation loss in full fine-tuning.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Extending fine-tuning past the validation-loss early-stopping point can improve downstream F1 when loss and F1 decouple, depending on the number of trainable parameters.

record.problems: The evidence is validation NER F1, not held-out pretraining loss. Model-size comparisons are not controlled scaling sweeps, and some combine architecture, training duration, or hyperparameter tuning. No uncertainty estimates are reported; the paper notes that the Dev dataset is small and uses a separate Validation dataset.
record.rows_left_out: Table 2 results for adapter-fusion, GPT-3 contexts or entities, and the CRF head, and Table 3 submission scores were left out because they do not report outcomes of model-size or compute scaling. The comparisons involving context changes concern a separate intervention.

untested.parts: No pretraining loss and no power-law fits.
No shape comparison at fixed parameter count.
No power-law form fitted for fine-tuning or transfer; only a few F1 points.
No controlled scale series, no relation to pretraining loss, no prediction of downstream F1.
No exponents or fitting choices compared.

missing.what: adapter-no-early result (63.4%, equal to adapter-baseline): longer training gave no gain with adapters. This is the counterpart to R6 that the authors discuss.
missing.versions: none (fine-tuning duration; relevant to fits_no_version entry)

record.verdict_notes: The reader's tests/T3 classification and V6 labels are overturned. The study applies a loose notion of scaling laws as an engineering heuristic. Its comparisons mix model family, pretraining data, trainable fraction, fine-tuning duration and hyperparameter tuning. It has no uncertainty estimates and only one run per configuration. The paper's mention of Kaplan et al. is a citation, not a replication.

versions.untested_parts: No held-out pretraining loss measurements or power-law fits in parameters, tokens, or compute.
No small-run fits or predictions of larger-run losses.
No fixed-compute allocation sweep or measurement of optimal parameter and token counts.
No controlled comparison of depth, width, or architecture at fixed parameter count.
Although the study fine-tunes language models, it does not test whether the same power-law form holds in fine-tuning or another training regime.
Reports downstream NER F1 comparisons across model sizes and training duration, but does not establish a predictive relationship to pretraining loss or fit a scale-to-performance curve.
Does not compare fitted exponents or compute-optimal splits across counting, schedule, data, or fitting choices, or test for curves bending away from a power law.

rows.subject: bert-base-uncased (adapter-baseline)
rows.operation_detail: Reported as the smaller-model reference in comparisons with xlm-roberta-large.
rows.note: The paper reports this score but does not give a controlled scale-to-performance fit.
rows.check: Single-model reference F1 for the authors' own system, not a measure of predictable scaling.

rows.subject: xlm-roberta-large (adapter-baseline-large)
rows.operation_detail: Compared adapter training on this larger model with the bert-base-uncased adapter baseline.
rows.note: The larger model has a slightly higher reported score; architecture and trainable parameter count also differ.
rows.check: BERT-base vs XLM-R-large adapter comparison (63.4→64.0). Two points only. It is confounded by different pretraining corpora and objectives and by different trainable-parameter shares (0.8% vs 4.3%). It cannot show predictability with scale.

rows.subject: bert-base-uncased (full-no-context-baseline)
rows.operation_detail: Reported as a smaller-model reference in the full fine-tuning comparison with xlm-roberta-large.
rows.note: The comparison with the large model is not presented as a controlled scaling-law fit.
rows.check: Reference value for the system's own variant comparisons; duplicates R5.

rows.subject: xlm-roberta-large (full-baseline-large)
rows.operation_detail: Compared full fine-tuning on this larger model with the bert-base-uncased full fine-tuning baseline.
rows.note: The larger model's reported score is higher, but the models differ in architecture and the paper does not fit a predictive curve.
rows.check: Two different pretrained model families. This is a system-variant comparison, not a controlled scale sweep.

rows.subject: bert-base-uncased (full-no-context-baseline)
rows.operation_detail: Compared early-stopped fine-tuning with the longer-training full-no-early run.
rows.note: The paper says early stopping triggered too early; this score is the reference for R6.
rows.check: Duplicate of R3, used as the reference for the early-stopping comparison.

rows.subject: bert-base-uncased (full-no-early)
rows.operation_detail: Continued training without early stopping, allowing longer training than the baseline.
rows.note: The authors state that removing early stopping allowed longer training and a much better result; training compute is not quantified.
rows.check: Removing early stopping during fine-tuning (61.2→69.9) concerns fine-tuning duration and overfitting/early-stopping behaviour, not pretraining scale or loss. It does not measure any version. Better recorded under fits_no_version.

rows.subject: xlm-roberta-large (full-tuned-no-early)
rows.operation_detail: Increased model size and extended training time; the authors also tuned hyperparameters.

conditions.value: full fine-tuning without early stopping; hyperparameters tuned

rows.note: The paper reports this as its best score, but size, training duration, and hyperparameter tuning are not isolated from one another.
rows.check: Model swap, longer training and hyperparameter tuning are changed together; the baseline (R6) differs in all three. This is the system's best-run selection value, not a scaling test.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Reported model-size and longer-training comparisons on the Validation dataset
reader_labels.reason: F1 is higher in the reported larger-model comparisons and after longer training without early stopping (R2, R4, R6, R7).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Adapter model-size comparison and comparisons with non-matched training setups
reader_labels.reason: The adapter score rises only from 63.4% to 64.0%, and other model-size comparisons combine architecture, training-duration, or hyperparameter differences; these results do not demonstrate predictability (R1-R4, R7).
